lesson.title: Chasing the High End: Understanding Right Skew
lesson.summary: A right-skewed distribution has a longer tail stretching toward high values, which pulls the mean above the median and is the shape behind everyday examples like income and home prices.
lesson.body:
A distribution is skewed right when its tail, the thin stretched out portion of the graph, points toward the larger values on the right side of the number line, while most of the data bunches up on the left. This is the mirror image of left skew: the peak, where most observations sit, is on the low side, and a smaller number of unusually large values stretch out to form a long right tail. As with left skew, the name refers to where the tail points, not where the hump of the graph is tallest.

The logic connecting right skew to the relationship between mean and median works the same way it did for left skew, just flipped in direction. The median is resistant, it only reflects the position of a value once everything is sorted, so a handful of very large values sitting out in the right tail barely change it. The mean, however, is calculated from the actual size of every value, so those same large numbers pull the arithmetic average upward substantially. This produces a dependable rule: in a right-skewed distribution, the mean is larger than the median.

Home prices provide a clean illustration. Suppose six homes on a street sell for, in thousands of dollars, 180, 195, 200, 210, 220, and 900, the last being a large estate on the same street. Sorted, the data is already in order. With six values, the median is the average of the third and fourth: 200 and 210, giving 205. The mean is the total divided by six: 180 + 195 + 200 + 210 + 220 + 900 = 1,905, and 1,905 divided by 6 is 317.5. The mean of 317.5 sits far above the median of 205, because the single 900 value dragged the average up while the median stayed anchored near where most of the houses actually sold.

Right skew is extremely common in real world quantitative data, which is exactly why the median rather than the mean is usually reported for things like household income, home prices, and hospital billing amounts. A small number of very high earners, very expensive homes, or very large bills stretch the distribution's tail to the right without changing what a "typical" case looks like, and reporting the mean in these situations can be misleading to someone expecting a typical value.

The signature of right skew also carries over to a boxplot: the whisker and any flagged outliers on the high end stretch out much farther than on the low end, while the box itself, covering the middle 50 percent of the data, sits closer to the low side of the display. Waiting times at a busy restaurant follow the same pattern as home prices, most parties wait a short, similar amount of time, but a few unlucky parties wait far longer, stretching the tail to the right without dragging the bulk of the data along with it.

Recognizing right skew from a graph takes practice: look for a histogram with a tall cluster of bars on the left and a few isolated, shrinking bars trailing off to the right. Combined with the earlier ideas of symmetric distributions, where mean and median match, and left skew, where the mean falls below the median, you now have all three basic relationships between mean and median that show up throughout the rest of this course and connect directly to the center-of-distribution and spread-of-distribution concepts ahead.
